title: Late-eviction batcher scratchpad
content:
Context:
- Noticed ~15-30% sustained throughput drop (tokens/sec) on a few Dedicated pools starting 2026-01-18. Latency P95 rose slightly but tail exploded on long sequences.
- Hypothesis initially focused on prefill and kvcache sizing; further traces point to late eviction + batch window expansion behavior.

What I observed (high level):
- Under steady load, batch window occasionally grows from 8ms -> 80-200ms for several seconds, then collapses. During expansion period, effective token throughput/crunch decreases even though batch sizes look sane.
- Logs show repeated slab/kv eviction events right around the start of each window expansion cluster. Eviction spikes co-occur with host small GC-like pauses (not actual GC, but allocator churn).

Relevant telemetry snippets (prometheus-ish, sampled):
- query: rate(inference_tokens_generated[2m]) -> baseline 1.2e6 t/s, dropped to 8.4e5 t/s on 2026-01-18 03:11 UTC
- query: sum(rate(batcher_window_ms_count[1m])) by (instance, window_ms) -> spikes at window_ms=100-200 on affected hosts

Representative log excerpts (redacted):
- [2026-01-18T03:10:41Z] WARN batcher: window_expanded instance=host-09 reason=no_fill threshold_ms=8 -> 120
- [2026-01-18T03:10:42Z] ERROR allocator: evicting slab id=0x7f8e size=2.1MB reason=pressure tenant=team-foo
- [2026-01-18T03:10:42Z] INFO kvcache: evicted 453 keys (recent_hits=0) kv_bytes=1.9MB
- [2026-01-18T03:10:44Z] WARN batcher: draining late batcher-queue len=72 drain_time_ms=170

Commands & queries I ran (notes on results):
1) Pulled full trace for one host (host-09)
- kubectl logs -n runtime host-09 --since=30m | egrep "batcher|evict|kvcache|drain" > host09-trace.txt
- Observation: eviction lines consistently cluster within a 1-3s window before throughput drop.

2) Prometheus checks
- curl -g 'http://prom.svc:9090/api/v1/query?query=sum(rate(batcher_window_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le, instance)'
- Seeing heavy mass in buckets > 50ms on affected instances.

3) Replayed traffic locally into a dev pool with env toggles
- python tools/replay_trace.py --trace=host09-trace --target=dev-pool --scale=0.8
- With default allocator and kvcache=false, no window spikes -> suggests interaction with kvcache/allocator state.

4) Quick-fix toggles tried on a single canary host (host-canary-02)
- set BATCHER_WINDOW_MS=12 -> reduced window variability but increased average latency slightly; throughput improved ~6%
- set KV_EVICTION_THRESHOLD=0.85 -> fewer evictions but memory pressure rose and OOM risk for other tenants; short-term throughput +12%
- set ALLOCATOR_FRAGMENTATION_PENALTY=0.6 -> marginally smoother drain times

Hypotheses (ranked):
A) Late eviction cascade: periodic allocator pressure (large rare allocations + small fragmentation) triggers mass kvcache evictions. Eviction causes cache misses on frequently used KV entries, causing more request work and preventing batches from filling on time -> windows expand to wait for more arrivals, but arrivals are slowed by extra work -> negative feedback loop.
B) Batcher drain logic asymmetry: when queue length hits a threshold during eviction storms, drain path forces early flushes with long drain_time_ms (drain stalls), which pushes more concurrency off the fast path and exacerbates serializing ops.
C) Tenant skew/noisy neighbor: a single tenant in the affected pool performs occasional large-seq requests that allocate many per-token temp buffers, causing allocator churn and slab compaction; other tenants suffer throughput collapse.

Experiment matrix (params tried so far):
- batcher_window_ms: 8, 12, 20
- kv_eviction_threshold: 0.6, 0.75, 0.85
- prefill_kv: 0, 1
- allocator_fragmentation_penalty: 0.3, 0.6
- result metric: tokens/sec (1m average), P95 latency, eviction_count/min

Results summary (canary runs):
- Lowering batcher_window_ms to 12 prevented some window expansions and gave +6% throughput; P95 increased ~10-20ms.
- Raising kv_eviction_threshold to 0.85 reduced eviction_count by ~70% in short runs, tokens/sec up +12% but memory headroom reduced alarmingly.
- Enabling prefill_kv=1 (prefetch small hot keys into working set when batch starts) helped reduce per-request extra work after eviction; combined with window_ms=12 showed best steady improvement of ~18% throughput recovery on canary for 30m run.

Commands to reproduce the best canary config locally:
- export BATCHER_WINDOW_MS=12
- export KV_EVICTION_THRESHOLD=0.85
- export PREFILL_KV=1
- ./bin/runtime --config path/to/dev-config.yml &
- python tools/replay_trace.py --trace=host09-trace --target=localhost:8080 --scale=0.8

Failure/error snippets to be aware of:
- "allocator: evicting slab ... reason=pressure" -> indicates memory pressure path; correlate with per-process RSS and slab fragmentation.
- "batcher: window_expanded ... reason=no_fill" -> means batcher didn't see enough arrivals in the configured window.
- "drain_time_ms=XXX" > 100ms -> triggers tailing throughput collapse if repeated.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why does eviction cluster periodically rather than being evenly distributed? Is there a periodic background job (compaction, model warmup, tracing) that aligns with requests?
- Are certain model variants causing temporary spikes of allocations (attention cache growth)? Map traces by model id.
- Is Redis/remote-kv interaction causing synchronous stalls during eviction (if we prefetch and eviction happens we might be falling back to remote).

Next steps (short-term):
1) Run 6-hour canary with combined best settings (window_ms=12, prefill_kv=1, kv_threshold=0.8) on a small subset of affected dedicated hosts. Monitor memory alarms closely.
2) Add temporary tracing on allocator events to capture full stack size and allocation histograms at the time of eviction (low-overhead sampling).
3) Correlate tenant request sizes & model_id distribution to eviction windows (query request logs for top 5 tenants in that pool).
4) Draft a mitigation PR: more conservative default batch window on hosts with high eviction_count, optional per-tenant isolation policy. Link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/789

Notes to self: keep experiment runs long enough (>=30m) to capture the episodic eviction spikes. Short microbench runs hide cascade. Also be wary of memory alarms when increasing kv thresholds — better to pair with per-tenant caps.

Slack snippets saved: 
- @arjun 'if we can prefill hot keys we reduce the extra per-request work post-evict'
- @maya 'we should not use global kv_threshold bump without limiting tenant OOM risk'

If this evolves into an incident report: include timeline, canary config, PR link, and a section with recommended permanent fixes: allocator backpressure smoothing, per-tenant working-set limits, and batcher asymmetry fix (drain path rework).

End of scratchpad.
